voice.persona: an experienced My Clinic colleague coaching a learner in their first week

segments.narration: OMAR: Welcome to RCM Part A: Documentation & Coding. You will practise decisions that help you act with confidence. You will leave with practical actions for your next shift.
segments.on_screen_text: "Documentation & coding that gets approved" · "RCM Part A"

segments.narration: OMAR: The reviewer only has your note. Good documentation protects the patient, you and the clinic. Keep the main point connected to a familiar task or conversation. That connection makes the information easier to use when it matters. Use the principle in context. Keep the next action clear. Think of the first detail you would check. Apply the point to a familiar task. Carry the idea into your next decision.
segments.on_screen_text: "The payer doesn't see your patient. The payer sees your note." · Clinical decision + documentation + coding = optimised payment

segments.narration: OMAR: This reflection is not scored. Choose the response that helps you set one intention for your next shift.
segments.on_screen_text: "What do you think is the #1 cause of rejections at My Clinic?" (4 causes)

segments.narration: OMAR: What always goes in, what never should. Use the tabs as a short reference, not a checklist to race through. Notice which detail would guide your next conversation or decision. Apply the point to a familiar task. Carry the idea into your next decision. Pause and connect this to your role. Use the principle in context. Keep the next action clear. Think of the first detail you would check. Apply the point to a familiar task. Carry the idea into your next decision.
segments.on_screen_text: Always: chief complaint & HPI · relevant findings · link symptoms to the working diagnosis · labs/imaging when needed · Avoid: vague notes · diagnosis without support · copy-paste · "fatigue only", "body pain"

segments.narration: NOOR: Same patient, same fluids. One note gets paid. Use the comparison to separate a helpful detail from a potential problem. The important step is turning what you see into a clear response. Carry the idea into your next decision. Pause and connect this to your role. Use the principle in context. Keep the next action clear.
segments.on_screen_text: Before: "Patient given IV fluids." · After: "Dehydration signs (HR 112, dry mucosa) — IV fluids started for stabilisation." Rendered as two note cards (SVG)

segments.narration: OMAR: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.
segments.on_screen_text: Order: Chief complaint → HPI → relevant past history → clinical findings → assessment → plan with duration & follow-up

segments.on_screen_text: "Which note best justifies a CBC?" options: "Routine CBC" / "Fatigue" / "Fatigue for 6 weeks, pallor, menorrhagia — rule out anaemia" ✔ / "Patient requested blood test"

segments.narration: OMAR: Coding is clinical translation. Specific codes get accepted. Notice which part of the information you would need first in practice. segments.on_screen_text: Primary = main condition treated · Secondary = complexity · Specific code = higher acceptance · #1 rejection cause: non-specific symptom coding

segments.narration: OMAR: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.
segments.on_screen_text: Presentations ↔ codes (final codes per B4): "Vomiting + diarrhoea, 2 days, dehydration" ↔ gastroenteritis code · "Sore throat, fever, tonsillar exudate" ↔ J03 Acute tonsillitis · "Headache, BP 168/102 on two readings" ↔ I10 Hypertension · "Polyuria, HbA1c 8.1%" …

segments.narration: OMAR: Talk through the provisional diagnosis: honest about uncertainty, still specific. Follow the example one step at a time, then identify why the next step makes sense. The value is the reasoning you can carry into a similar case. Apply the point to a familiar task. Carry the idea into your next decision. Pause and connect this to your role. Use the principle in context. Keep the next action clear. Think of the first detail you would check. Apply the point to a familiar task. Carry the idea into your next decision.
segments.on_screen_text: Fever 3 days + dysuria + suprapubic pain → urinalysis and culture ordered → document a provisional diagnosis linked to the findings → confirm or change when results return. Self-explanation: "Why is a provisional diagnosis better than 'fever' here?"

segments.narration: OMAR: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose. Feedback explains the reasoning after you respond.
segments.on_screen_text: Items: E66 Obesity (BMI 31) · L70 Acne · L66 Hair loss · L21 Seborrhoeic dermatitis · N97 Female infertility · General check-up · J03 Acute tonsillitis · E11 Type 2 diabetes · Obesity with BMI 42 referred for bariatric …

segments.narration: OMAR: Defensive medicine feels safe but gets rejected. Follow work-up protocols, document deviations. As you read, focus on the decision this information supports in your own role. The aim is a practical next action, not a phrase to memorise. Pause and connect this to your role. Use the principle in context. Keep the next action clear. Think of the first detail you would check. Apply the point to a familiar task. Carry the idea into your next decision.
segments.on_screen_text: Follow initial work-up protocols · No supplements without indication · Repeat only at evidence-based intervals · If you deviate, document why

segments.narration: OMAR: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose. Focus on the action that fits. Feedback explains the reasoning after you respond. Use the rule you practised.
segments.on_screen_text: Node 1: 45-year-old with multi-joint pain, first visit, no history → order everything (CRP, ESR, anti-DNA, anti-Ro, anti-La) vs initial work-up (CRP, ESR) ✔. Node 2: same patient, rheumatoid arthritis already diagnosed by a rheumatologist elsewhere → document the history …

segments.on_screen_text: "Your diabetic patient's HbA1c was done 6 weeks ago. He asks for another." Best action → don't repeat yet unless there's a documented clinical reason; next test at the approved interval (B3)

segments.narration: OMAR: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.
segments.on_screen_text: "Prescribing a combined multivitamin 'for general wellness' with no documented deficiency is likely to be rejected." → True (B8)

segments.on_screen_text: Rejection notes → causes: "No indication for the MRI" → missing justification · "Diagnosis: fever" → non-specific · "No examination findings recorded" → incomplete · "Antibiotic billed for a viral URTI code" → mismatch (+ 4 more)

segments.on_screen_text: Benefits are added and amended often · Know what's covered, adapt documentation · "If you don't document it properly, it won't be covered — even if it's clinically correct." · Next: Part B covers the new EBP
